skills.name: The accounting cycle: journal, ledger and trial balance

note.text:
Accounting cycle: source documents (invoices, receipts) → journal → ledger → trial balance → financial statements.
• Journal: transactions recorded in date order, each with the accounts debited and credited, amounts and a short explanation.
• Ledger: each account on its own page (T-account); journal amounts are posted to the debit or credit side.
• Balance of an account = difference between its debit total and credit total (debit balance if debits are bigger).
• Trial balance: a list of all account balances; total debit balances must equal total credit balances. If not, there is an error.

sections.heading: From documents to statements
sections.text:
Every transaction starts with a source document: an invoice, a receipt, a bank statement. The accounting cycle then follows:
source documents → journal → ledger → trial balance → financial statements (balance sheet and income statement).

sections.heading: Journal and ledger
sections.text:
The journal records transactions in date order. Each entry gives the date, the account(s) debited and credited, the amounts and a short description; the debits equal the credits.
The ledger has one page (a T-account) for each account. Posting means copying each journal amount to the same side of the right ledger account.
The balance of an account is the difference between its two sides: a debit balance if the debits are bigger, a credit balance if the credits are bigger.

sections.heading: Trial balance
sections.text:
A trial balance lists every account with its balance, debit balances in one column and credit balances in the other. The two totals must be equal.
If they differ, there is an error (a one-sided posting, a wrong addition). But equal totals do not prove everything is right: an entry left out completely, or posted to the wrong account on the correct side, does not show up.

key_words.meaning: book of first entry, in date order
book of accounts, one page per account
copying journal amounts to the ledger
list of balances to check that debits equal credits

mistake.right: Balance = the larger side − the smaller side
mistake.why: A balance is the difference between the two sides.

worked_example.problem: The Bank account has debits of {a} FCFA and {b} FCFA and a credit of {c} FCFA. Find its balance.
steps: Balance = {a + b} − {c} = {a + b - c} FCFA (a debit balance).

cards.idea: The balance is the difference between the two sides of an account.
In a trial balance, debit and credit totals must agree.
example: If they differ, look for an error.

check.prompt: A trial balance shows debit balances of {x}, {y} and {z} FCFA and credit balances of {u} and {v} FCFA. By how much do the totals differ (FCFA)? (0 if they agree)

misconceptions.explain: That is the debit total. Compare it with the credit total.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of the accounting cycle in order.
An account has debits totalling {d} FCFA and credits totalling {c} FCFA. What is the size of its balance (FCFA)?

misconceptions.explain: The balance is the difference between the sides, not their sum.

pick.r: Transferring journal amounts to the ledger accounts
e: That is a transaction, not posting.
pick.y: Each journal line goes to its ledger account.

pick.q: A journal entry debits 571 Cash and credits 701 Sales with 25 000 FCFA. How is it posted?
pick.r: 25 000 on the debit side of Cash and on the credit side of Sales
w: 25 000 on the credit side of Cash
25 000 on the debit side of Sales
e: Each account gets the amount once, on its own side.
pick.y: Post each amount to the same side as in the journal.

pick.q: Which document is the starting point of the accounting cycle?
pick.r: source documents such as invoices and receipts
e: The ledger comes after the journal.
pick.y: Every entry must be supported by a document.

pick.q: A trial balance agrees. Does that prove there are no errors?
pick.r: No: some errors (such as a wrong account or a missing entry) do not affect the totals
w: No, a trial balance never agrees
pick.y: Errors of omission or of principle leave the totals equal.

pick.q: Rent of 50 000 FCFA was paid in cash but posted only to the Rent account. What happens to the trial balance?
pick.r: It does not agree: debits exceed credits by 50 000
e: The debit was posted, the credit was not.

pick.q: Why do debit and credit totals agree in a correct trial balance?
pick.r: Every transaction was recorded with equal debits and credits
w: Because Cash is always the largest account
Because there are always ten accounts
pick.y: Double entry keeps the books in balance.
